birth.stop: Würzburg, the country the Latin gives away
birth.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year is an ordering device only. No document names Adam's birthplace, his parents, or his year of birth. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin and the Neue Deutsche Biographie both place his origin in eastern Franconia or western Thuringia, perhaps near Würzburg, arguing from name forms, his attention to the Main-country missionary saints, and verbal affinities with Main-Werra material. The sources say only 'probably before c. 1050'. An early scholium in manuscript C2, itself perhaps of 1085-1090 or later, says the author came from Germania superior, Upper Germany, and no more.

stops.stop: Bamberg, the cathedral school that may have made him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the source that proposes it disclaims it. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin states that whether Adam visited the then famous cathedral school of Bamberg cannot be assured. The contents of his education are inferred securely from the Gesta itself; the building he sat in is not. The 1065 correspondence between Bamberg clergy and Archbishop Adalbert is real but has never been shown to be his road north.

stops.stop: Magdeburg, the school an older tradition gave him
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and a contradiction left standing. English Wikipedia states flatly that Adam is believed to have come from Meissen and that it is probable he was taught at the Magdeburger Domschule. Modern specialist synthesis treats this Upper Saxon line as superseded by the Franconia and Thuringia hypothesis. Neither is documented. The attribution of the Meissen hypothesis to Wilhelm Wattenbach, which circulates in some summaries, could not be verified in Tschan or the NDB and is not repeated here.

stops.date_confidence: attested with a caveat the sources themselves supply. A charter of 11 June 1069 was written and signed for Adalbert by an Adam magister scolarum. stops.stop: Bremen, Rimbert's books on the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested as source-dependence, undated as an event. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin identifies the anonymous Vita Rimberti and Rimbert's own Vita Anskarii as Adam's material for Gesta I.34-44. Rimbert's lost letter to Ratramnus of Corbie, sent before 865, is attested through Ratramnus's surviving reply. There is no surviving evidence that Adam had that reply in front of him when he wrote the cynocephali passage of Book IV, and this file does not claim he did.

stops.stop: Bremen, an archive that had forged its own foundation
stops.date_confidence: attested as method, reconstruction as to Adam's state of mind. stops.stop: Bremen, the body borne from Goslar
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested verbatim, the location of Adam is not. Gesta III.lxvii(66): 'Our most illustrious metropolitan Adalbert died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April in the tenth Indiction. That was the year of our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand and seventy-two.' III.lxviii(67) has the body borne from Goslar to Bremen. The claim repeated in some reference works that Adam attended the deathbed is supported by no passage placing him at Goslar, and is not carried here. The stop sits at Bremen because that is where Adam demonstrably was.

stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Schmeidler's compositional analysis, relayed by Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, and a contradiction left standing. stops.stop: Bremen, the archbishop under sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested as external history, reconstruction as to its bearing on the text. Liemar, archbishop 1072-1101 and the Gesta's dedicatee, supported Henry IV, was excommunicated by Gregory VII in 1075, and was absolved at Canossa in 1077. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin treats this as the political backdrop of Adam's continued revision. Adam himself never mentions the quarrel, and he is not recorded anywhere near Canossa.

stops.segment: Beyond the Danes: Sweden, Norway, and the Ice
stops.stop: Vinland, an island the king names
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.xxxix(38), tr. Tschan, and as the earliest surviving written European notice of Vinland. Adam gives no coordinates and no sailing directions; the pin is a placeholder in the western ocean for the report itself. He did not go, names no captain and no year, and attributes the whole of it to the Danes. L'Anse aux Meadows, excavated by the Ingstads from 1961 after Helge Ingstad located it in 1960, is the only confirmed Norse site in North America and is a modern hypothesis about the sagas, not about Adam.

stops.segment: Beyond the Danes: Sweden, Norway, and the Ice
stops.stop: The frozen sea, the edge of the record
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.40, tr. Tschan; the place is not a place. Adam gives no coordinates for the numbing ocean and its whirling current, which is a classical topos of the world's edge. The pin is symbolic, set in the North Atlantic beyond Iceland along the line the Frisian story runs, and it maps a passage of writing rather than a location.

stops.stop: Bremen, the last correction
stops.date_confidence: attested as a negative fact. The NDB gives about 1081 as the end of Adam's own additions and 1085 as the latest possible year of his death; Tschan writes that after 1085 there is no trace of Adam's hand in the text or scholia. The range sometimes given as 1085-90 is not supported by any source checked here; every source stops at 1085.

stops.stop: Bremen, magister Adam, the twelfth of October
stops.date_confidence: the day is attested, the year is not, and the place is inference. Tschan: 'In the Dyptichon Bremense a magister Adam is noted as having died on October 12, but, as was the rule in such records, without mention of the year.' Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin gives 12 October in an unknown year between 1081 and 1085. The file dates the stop 1085-10-12 only to place it last in sequence. No source states a place of death or a burial site; Bremen is inferred from residence, and the grave is a documented gap.

stops.stop: Leiden, the oldest surviving leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested. Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek, Voss. Lat. Q. 123 (siglum A2), copied around 1100, containing excerpts from Gesta II.16-22 and Book IV on leaves later cut down by a binder, is the oldest surviving witness; the Leiden catalogue record carries the description. That Book IV began circulating separately from about 1100 is reported by Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin. Adam's own manuscript does not survive in any form.

stops.stop: Copenhagen, the first printing
stops.date_confidence: attested, and it corrects a claim in wide circulation. Tschan's introduction is explicit: 'Of the printings already noted, those of B2 by Vedel in 1579 and of C2 by Lindenbrog in 1595, only the latter was republished.' Danish sources confirm Vedel issued the first printed edition of Adam's church history in 1579, at Copenhagen. German Wikipedia's article on the Gesta names Lindenbrog's 1595 Leiden printing as the first edition; that contradiction is flagged and resolved in Tschan's favour, and the resolution is stated rather than assumed.

stops.stop: Copenhagen, codex z burns
stops.date_confidence: attested as a loss, approximate as a day. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin records that codex z, a B-family manuscript of 1161/62, was destroyed in the Copenhagen fire of 1728 and survives only partially through later copies. The fire ran from 20 to 23 October 1728; the stop takes its first day.

stops.stop: Hannover, the three lost states
stops.date_confidence: attested. Johann Martin Lappenberg edited the Gesta for MGH Scriptores VII in 1846, working from A1; Bernhard Schmeidler's edition of 1917 in the MGH Scriptores rerum Germanicarum in usum scholarum remains the scholarly standard and reconstructs three lost authorial states, A, a and X. Tschan's English translation appeared from Columbia University Press in 1959. The Vienna manuscript ÖNB Cod. 521 (A1), long dated to around 1200, is dated by German Wikipedia to the first half of the thirteenth century.
